source.title: The Geometry of Over-parameterized Regression and Adversarial Perturbations

record.file_problem: none; full paper and supporting information are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests double descent using geometric analysis and simulations of minimal linear-regression and random-feature models, rather than the original deep-network settings.
record.gate_note: The study reports test-error and geometric bias/variance results relevant to double descent. Its adversarial-perturbation results do not measure any listed claim version and are omitted. Values used to construct schematic figures are not treated as separate outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study simulates test error against Np/M in ridgeless OLS models and decomposes it into geometric bias and variance. The models are no-basis linear regression and two-layer random-feature networks with a fixed middle layer. It is a different method (feature-space geometry plus minimal-model simulations) aimed at the model-wise double-descent question, and is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors offer an input-feature-space geometric interpretation of double descent: misaligned subspaces (θmax→90°) produce a geometric-variance divergence at interpolation, and falling geometric bias improves the over-parameterized regime. They argue double descent can occur without label noise, but this rests on the noise-free geometric error and cited prior work, not a noise-free simulation. They also tie adversarial directions to model bias.
record.recipe_differences: Uses OLS and random-feature regression with a geometric feature-space analysis; it is not the original deep-network or sample-wise experimental recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The study considers no-basis, random linear-feature, and random nonlinear-feature models. It reports a fixed ReLU numerical example and a fixed label signal-to-noise ratio; it does not systematically vary noise or regularization.

fits_no_version.finding: Near the interpolation threshold the subspace orientation angle θmax approaches 90° and δφmax approaches 0°. The feature operator Pf then becomes nearly an oblique projector, which the authors tie to the variance peak.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The double-descent peak coincides with misalignment between the subspace the model can express and the subspace spanned by the training data.

record.problems: The numerical evidence concerns minimal regression models, including two-layer networks with a random fixed middle layer, rather than end-to-end-trained deep networks. Several supporting-information outcomes are presented only in plots without explicit values or textual descriptions. The numerical example uses a fixed signal-to-noise ratio and regularization setting.
record.rows_left_out: The study also plots training error, geometric test error, geometric bias, and additional geometric or matrix quantities in Figures S5–S7. They were not added where they do not independently measure a listed claim version or where they duplicate the model-size test-error result. Adversarial-perturbation outcomes in Figure 4 are outside the listed versions.

untested.parts: No deep networks trained end-to-end. Only fixed-middle-layer random-feature and linear models are used.
No sweep over epochs or training time.
No sample-size sweep. M is fixed at 512 and only Np/M is varied.
Only least-squares regression classes (linear, random linear features, random ReLU features). No kernels, trees or classification.
No test of a single effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across axes.

Label noise is not varied: there is a single SNR of 10. The noise-free claim is argued via the geometric error definition and prior work [34], not a noise-free simulation. There is no multiple-peak analysis and no regularization tuning, since λ is fixed at 1e-8.
No recounting of parameters by an effective number of parameters.

missing.what: Training and test error vs Np/M for OLS. The text states test error follows a classical U-shape below the threshold and decreases above it while training error stays zero.
Geometric bias decreases monotonically with Np, explaining better over-parameterized performance.

record.verdict_notes: Mainly a theoretical and geometric paper; the numerical evidence for double descent is Fig. 1(a) and Fig. 3(a) in one random ReLU-feature setup averaged over at least 500 simulations. The reader's V1 labels were moved to V4, because no deep network is trained. The adversarial-perturbation results (Fig. 4) are outside all versions.

versions.untested_parts: Tests model-size double descent in minimal regression models, including two-layer networks with random fixed middle layers; it does not test deep networks trained end-to-end.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
No sample-size sweep examining whether more training data raises test error near interpolation.
Tests several minimal regression model classes, not a broad range of model classes or the full classical U-shaped-to-double-descent account.
The paper gives a geometric account using subspace angles and singular values, but does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and samples.

Reports geometric variance at the interpolation peak and argues double descent can occur without label noise. Does not test multiple or triple peaks, vary noise systematically, or compare optimally tuned regularization.
Does not recast parameter count using an effective number of parameters or test whether that makes the second descent an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.measure: Test error Etest; authors report a double-descent profile with divergence at the interpolation threshold and better performance in the over-parameterized than under-parameterized regime.
rows.value: double-descent profile; test error diverges at the interpolation threshold; over-parameterized regime performs better than its under-parameterized counterpart
rows.uncertainty: Small error bars indicate error on the mean; exact values not stated.
rows.note: The authors say the divergence in geometric test error stems from geometric variance at interpolation and that decreasing geometric bias improves the over-parameterized regime. The model is a two-layer random-feature network with a fixed middle layer.
rows.check: Subject is a random-feature regression with a fixed, untrained middle layer, not a deep network trained end-to-end. It bears on V4 (non-deep model classes), not V1. The V6 link is better carried by r2, since r1 measures total test error rather than what drives the peak.
